details:
ELON MARS — Explore, Observe, Discover

ELON MARS is a browser-based 3D educational game that introduces young learners to Mars science through exploration. Players travel across a fictional Martian landscape on foot or scout ahead with an independently controlled rover, investigating natural features and recording their discoveries.

The game includes five regions inspired by Martian geology: impact craters, subsurface ice, volcanic terrain, ancient lake sediments, and wind-shaped dunes. Across these regions, players can discover 15 scientific features. Approaching a feature displays an inspection prompt; pressing F opens a scientific information card containing an accessible explanation, NASA mission context, source attribution, and evidence limitations.

Our central learning loop is explore, observe, inspect, and record. A field codex saves discoveries locally, while completing a regional survey earns a supply package for air, meals, and energy. This connects scientific investigation with simple resource-management decisions. A minimap supports navigation, and third-person controls, jumping, and physical collisions make exploration interactive.

NASA resources inform explanations of crater ejecta, buried water ice, carbon-dioxide frost, lava flows and tubes, ancient volcanic eruptions, sedimentary deltas, dust devils, and wind streaks. We clearly distinguish these published observations from the game’s authored teaching models. The fictional landscapes are not measured NASA locations, and the game does not claim real-time weather, confirmed mineral identifications, present-day volcanic activity, or evidence of life.

We developed the project using TypeScript, React, Three.js, React Three Fiber, Vite, Tailwind CSS, and Zustand. Procedural geometry and materials create the environments, while browser storage preserves progress without requiring an account. Keyboard and touch interfaces are included. Development considerations included readable scientific explanations, reliable inspection distances, camera visibility, collision behavior, and maintaining separate control of the explorer and rover.

The project addresses the Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer challenge by transforming Mars science into an active investigation. Its intended impact is to encourage curiosity, observation, and evidence-based reasoning, helping learners understand not only what scientists know about Mars, but also how observations support—or limit—a scientific conclusion.

AI-use acknowledgement: AI assistants supported planning, code development, debugging, test creation, and documentation. The team directed development and remains responsible for reviewing and validating the submitted work. NASA references are credited separately.
